catalog_quote: 3.1. Primary stress in monomorphemes. The basic primary stress pattern of Samoan is simple: a moraic trochee at the right edge of the word (Homer 2007a). Stress is on the last vowel if long, and otherwise on the second-to-last. Examples are given in (4), with parentheses enclosing presumed feet, and acute accent marking primary stress. (4) Basic primary stress pattern: moraic trochee at right edge ... la(vá:) 'energized' ... le(léi) 'good' ... (mánu) 'bird' ... ma(nó i) 'to smell good' ... Samoan primary stress is similar to Fijian (Dixon 1988; Schütz 1978, 1985), where, in Hayes's (1995) analysis, a word ends with a moraic trochee. In both Fijian and Samoan, there are no surface forms with a short final vowel and a long penultimate vowel (e.g., *[má:nu])—see Section 5. We will see a systematic set of exceptions to the basic pattern in Section 7. ... 3.3. Analysis of basic primary stres…
sweep_summary: Samoan (samo1305) is in the catalog as 'weight' on Zuraw, Yu & Orfitelli 2014 (right-edge moraic trochee: final if long vowel/diphthong, else penult), corroborated by Pratt 1893. Of the five searched titles, two are first-hand word-accent studies that could not be obtained: Condax 1990 'Locative accent in Samoan' (Oceanic Linguistics 29(1): 27-48, DOI 10.2307/3623203, JSTOR-only; priority high, because a locative-conditioned accent shift would refine the morphology note) and Schütz 2007 'Accent patterns for English loanwords in Samoan' (Benjamins CLL 30: 133-146, DOI 10.1075/cll.30.16sch, paywalled, no abstract exposed; priority medium). The other three are sentence-level prosody: Yu 2011 (NELS 39; downloaded from the author's site and read) is about an absolutive H- boundary tone but its §2 states the word-stress rule verbatim and confirms the catalog; Calhoun 2015 (Lingua, closed, not read) and Calhoun, Clemens & Elfner 2017 (Glossa, gold OA but the site's Anubis bot-wall blocked every PDF URL by automated download; abstract read) concern focus marking and prosodic phrasing, silent on stress placement. Two on-disk Yu papers (Prosodic Typology III preprint §12.1.1; Formal Grammar 2017) were also read and confirm the classification, adding the aea/aoa VVV antepenultimate exception. Nothing read supersedes Zuraw et al. 2014; catalog record stands. Glottolog 631804 mis-lists the NELS 39 editors (Lima, Mullin, Smith) as co-authors of Yu 2011. All downloads and non-downloads.

new_statements.reading: Word stress is weight-sensitive: a bimoraic trochee at the right word edge, so primary stress on a final long vowel or diphthong and otherwise on the penultimate syllable; secondary stress on preceding trochees; an LH pitch accent marks the stressed mora. Identical to the catalog's 'weight' coding (final-if-heavy-else-penult). Based on the same UCLA fieldwork (2008-09) as Zuraw, Yu & Orfitelli 2014, so it is corroboration by a co-author, not an independent source.

tone_statements.quote: The basic footing pattern, as observed in monomorphemes, consists of a moraic trochee at the right edge of the word (Zuraw et al. 2014). Primary stress is on the final vowel if it's long, and otherwise on the penultimate vowel. Further details on Samoan stress assignment are in Zuraw et al. (2014). Primary stress is associated with a pitch accent, which is consistently phonetically realized with increased relative amplitude, longer duration, and a rise in fundamental frequency (f0). [...] an Habs carries morphemic contrast between absolutive vs. other cases in Samoan and if segmental case markers are dropped, can be the only signal of this contrast. audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Zuraw, Yu & Orfitelli 2014 eprint at the stated section/page (sec. 3.1, ms p. 6; sec. 7.1 for the diphthong exceptions), and the corroborating Pratt 1893 passage is verbatim at Grammar pp. 2-3 in the held archive.org text. The classification (weight-sensitive, right edge, moraic trochee: final stress iff final V: or diphthongising ai/au/ei/ou, else penult; secondary trochees leftward) rests on the best available source - a dedicated 2014 Phonology article with instrumental f0 evidence - and two later open works by co-author Yu downloaded now (Prosodic Typology III preprint ch. 12; FG 2017) restate exactly this rule and report that Mosel & Hovdhaugen 1992 p. 28 and Churchward 1951 pp. 9, 24 agree. Nothing found suggests a different coding; the unheld reference grammar would only add corroboration.

sources.citation: Yu, Kristine M. 2011. The sound of ergativity: morphosyntax-prosody mapping in Samoan. In Suzi Lima, Kevin Mullin & Brian Smith (eds.), Proceedings of NELS 39, 825-838. [Glottolog 631804 lists Lima, Mullin & Smith as co-authors; the PDF's author line is Kristine M. Yu (UCLA) alone.]
sources.quote: Samoan is an intonational language without lexically contrastive tone. Stress is quantity-sensitive, with long vowels and diphthongs counting as heavy, and the basic primary stress pattern aligns moraic trochees at the right edge (Zuraw et al. 2008), e.g. ma(líni) 'marine', (mànu)(má:) 'dove'. Describing the intonational system in terms of the autosegmental-metrical framework (Ladd 1996, i.a.), the default pitch accent that occurs in each content word is a LH rise over the mora receiving primary stress (Orfitelli and Yu 2008), and declaratives end in utterance final low tones.
sources.locator: §2 'A brief overview of Samoan prosody', p. 2 of the PDF (txt ll. 60-70)
sources.note: The paper is about a high boundary tone (H-) at the left edge of absolutive arguments (phrasal/morphosyntactic tone), but its one-paragraph prosody overview states the word-stress rule: quantity-sensitive, long vowels and diphthongs heavy, right-edge moraic trochee, i.e. final if long/diphthong, otherwise penult ((mànu)(má:) 'dove', ma(líni) 'marine'), with an LH pitch accent on the primary-stressed mora. Cites Zuraw, Orfitelli & Yu 2008 (AFLA XV talk), the precursor of the catalog's deciding source.

sources.citation: Pratt, George (1893). A grammar and dictionary of the Samoan language. Samoa: London Missionary Society's Press. viii+416 pp.
sources.quote: Accent. The general rule is that the accent is on the penultima, but to this there are exceptions. Many words ending in a long vowel take the accent on the ultima; as ma‘elegā, zealous; ‘onā, to be intoxicated; faigatā, difficult. Verbs formed from nouns ending in a, and meaning to abound in, have properly two a’s, as puaā (pua‘aa), ponā, tagatā, but are written with one. In speaking of a place at some distance, the accent is placed on the last syllable; as ‘O lo‘o i Safotū, he is at Safotu. The same thing is done in referring to a family; as sa Muliagā, the family of Muliaga. So most words ending in ga, not a sign of a noun, as tigā, puapuagā, pologā, fantagā, ugā. So also all words ending in a diphthong, as mamau, mafai, aoai. ... When a word receives an addition by means of an affixed particle, the accent is shifted forward; as alófa, love; alofága, loving, or showing love; alofagía, beloved. Reduplicated words have two accents; as pálapála, mud; ségiségi, twilight.
sources.locator: Grammar pp. 2-3, 'Accent' (archive.org item agrammaranddict00pratgoog: PDF pp. 15-16; djvu text ll. 684-720)
sources.note: Held by the project since 2026-09-20 ( and, lexical-bibliography pass) and read: the record itself co-cites this 'Accent' passage (Grammar pp. 2-3) as corroboration and the audit verified it verbatim. A first-hand 19th-century grammar, independent of Zuraw, Yu & Orfitelli 2014: penultimate accent by default, ultima accent when the word ends in a long vowel or a diphthong, accent shifting rightward under suffixation, i.e. the catalog's right-edge weight-sensitive coding. Quote transcribed from the page images (PDF pp. 15-16); the djvu OCR of the same lines is garbled ('penoltima', 'ma^eHega').

sources.citation: Calhoun, Sasha. 2017. Exclusives, equatives and prosodic phrases in Samoan. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 2(1): 11, 1-43. doi:10.5334/gjgl.196
sources.quote: Lexical stress usually falls on the penultimate mora (Zuraw et al. 2014). [p. 3] ... Each prosodic word in Samoan is usually associated with a rising pitch accent, L+H*, i.e. an L (low) pitch target rising to a peak associated with the stressed mora, H* ... The stressed mora is usually penultimate (Zuraw et al. 2014), i.e. when the final vowel in the word is short, the peak is associated with the penultimate vowel (e.g. with /le/ in meleni in Figure 2), whereas when the final vowel is long, the peak is associated with that vowel (e.g. with /la:/ in analeila in Figure 3). [p. 18] ... In a few cases, secondary lexical stress is also marked with a pitch accent, so there are two pitch accents in the prosodic word, e.g. on tausami in Figure 3. Secondary stress is usually marked with a (!)H* accent, but occasionally L+(!)H* (as was also found by Orfitelli & Yu 2009). [p. 19]
sources.note: Abstract only: the paper is about prosodic phrasing (H- phrase tones, phrase breaks) and information structure, not word-stress placement. It is gold open access (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar: GOLD, CC-BY) but every glossa-journal.org URL, including the Crossref-registered PDF galley, returned the Anubis 'Making sure you're not a bot' page by automated download; DOAJ record 403; web.archive.org could not be reached by automated download; not on LingBuzz.

sources.quote: This is a pitch accent associated to the penultimate syllable, which receives primary stress. The basic footing pattern in Samoan, as observed in monomorphemes, consists of a moraic trochee at the right edge of the word (Zuraw et al., 2014). Primary stress is on the final vowel if it is long, e.g., la(ˈvaː) ‘energized,’ and otherwise on the penultimate vowel, e.g., ma (ˈlini) ‘marine.’ Thus, ma(ˈlini) has a rising pitch accent associated to the penultimate syllable, where the low F0 valley appears around the onset of the stressed mora, and the high F0 peak appears at or slightly later than the offset of the stressed mora

sources.quote: The basic stress assignment pattern observed in native monomorphemes can be described as primary stress on the penultimate mora and analyzed with inviolable constraints enforcing trochaic, bimoraic feet within a prosodic word, e.g., ("manu) 'animal', ("la:) 'sun', with the the head foot aligned to the right edge of the prosodic word, e.g., ma("manu) 'design', (­sa:)("moa) 'Sāmoa' (Zuraw et al., 2014), see also Churchward (1951, p. 9, 24) and Mosel and Hovdhaugen (1992, p. 28). Exceptions come from stress on the antepenultimate mora in diphthongization of /ai, au, ei, ou/ VV sequences and additionally /aea/, /aoa/ VVV sequences, e.g., ("mai)le, *ma("ile) 'dog' but ma("ela), *("mae)la 'hollow', ("mae)a, *ma("ea) 'get'; see Zuraw et al. (2014, §8) for further details and analysis.
sources.note: Primary stress on the penultimate mora (right-aligned bimoraic trochee), so final stress when the last syllable is long (("la:)); diphthongising ai/au/ei/ou and aea/aoa sequences give antepenultimate-mora stress; secondary stress from further trochees; loanword secondary stress avoids epenthetic vowels; some intra-speaker variation in loans (taiamita). Cites Zuraw et al. 2014, Churchward 1951, Mosel & Hovdhaugen 1992. Restates the catalog's rule and adds the VVV-sequence exception detail. The author is a co-author of the catalog's own source (Zuraw, Yu & Orfitelli 2014), which this passage cit
